subtype: Approach: spotting weak topics and giving them extra time [Revision]
passage: In the school library after the mock round, Jahnavi and Ganga sat with the score sheet and their teacher watching quietly. "Look," said Ganga, pointing. "Three geography questions wrong." Jahnavi nodded. "Every time it's about rivers and states." They did not blame each other. They borrowed a big atlas from the shelf and a fold-out map. All week they spent twenty minutes a day quizzing each other on rivers, capitals and mountains, pointing at the map. In the next mock round, they missed only one geography question. Jahnavi high-fived Ganga, and even the teacher smiled.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi and Ganga borrow from the library?
qa.a: They borrowed a big atlas and a fold-out map.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi and Ganga feel about the wrong geography answers?
qa.a: They were disappointed but calm and practical, since they did not blame each other and made a plan instead.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use for geography, and why?
qa.a: They could ask the teacher for a list of the most likely topics or play a map game with a partner. Both would target the weak area quickly.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the team's improvement?
qa.a: The teacher watched quietly and smiled at the better score, so the teacher probably feels proud that the pair fixed their own weak spot.

grounding: After a mock round the team notices they miss geography questions, spends a week with a map and atlas, and their score improves.
